intuition: Scanning all positions finds a peak, but the required logarithmic time means we must discard a large part of the array after each comparison. Searching for the global maximum is unnecessary: any value greater than both neighbors is acceptable, including an endpoint with its outside neighbor treated as negative infinity.

Compare the middle value with the next value. A rise guarantees a peak somewhere to the right: either the rising run eventually falls, creating a local peak, or it reaches the final element. A fall guarantees a peak in the left part, including the middle itself.

Keep an inclusive candidate interval and preserve a side containing a peak at every update. Adjacent values are unequal, so the comparison always supplies a direction. When one index remains, the maintained boundary slopes ensure it is a valid peak. Multiple possible peaks do not require tie-breaking.

steps: For nums=[1,2,1,3,5,6,4], start with left=0 and right=6.
Midpoint 3 contains value 3, while index 4 contains 5. The slope rises, so keep the right side by setting left=4.
Now mid=5 contains 6 and index 6 contains 4. The slope falls; keep mid as a possible peak by setting right=5.
With interval [4,5], mid=4 contains 5 and its right neighbor contains 6. Set left=5.
Left and right now both equal 5, so stop without another neighbor comparison.
Return index 5. Its value 6 is greater than both neighbors, 5 and 4; the earlier peak at index 1 need not be found.

codeNotes.note: While left<right, this midpoint is strictly before right, so reading mid+1 remains inside the array.
A rising edge guarantees a peak beyond mid, allowing the entire left portion to be discarded.
A falling edge allows mid itself to be the peak. Keeping it avoids accidentally discarding the correct answer.
